title: Bhishma waits for the sun
hook: a single day of the creator lasts a thousand ages, and the universe breathes in and out with it
carry: the path of light and the path of smoke

segments.voice: Yesterday, sulabha: a king who died thinking of a fawn. Your line was: the last thought is made of every day. Today, the biggest clock in the Gita, at the end of chapter eight.

Bhishma, the great elder of the Mahabharata, falls in battle, pierced by so many arrows that his body rests on them like a bed. And he doesn't die. He had been given the power to choose his time. So he lies on the arrows for days, teaching, waiting. Waiting for what? For the sun to turn north: uttarayana, the sun's northern course. Only then, the story says, does he let go. Why would the sun's direction matter at the moment of death? The end of chapter eight is where that idea lives.
screen: `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `BHISHMA WAITS.` → `FOR THE SUN TO TURN NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, the enormous clock. Verse seventeen: those who know that a day of Brahma, the creator, lasts a thousand ages, and his night another thousand, truly know day and night. When Brahma's day dawns, all things come out of the unmanifest; when his night falls, they dissolve back into it. The whole universe breathing in and out. But, verse twenty, beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal, which doesn't perish when all beings perish. That's the highest goal; whoever reaches it doesn't return. Then the two paths, verses twenty-four and twenty-five. One: fire, light, day, the bright half of the moon, the six months of the sun's northern course. The knowers of Brahman who go by it reach Brahman. The other: smoke, night, the dark half of the moon, the six months of the southern course. Those who go by it reach the light of the moon, and return. Commentators read this differently. Some take it as the actual timing of death, and Bhishma's waiting fits that reading. Others read the markers as guides or stages on the soul's journey, the path of light and the path of smoke. Verse twenty-seven is clear either way: the yogi who knows these two paths isn't confused. And many Hindus still count the sun's turn north as an auspicious time, and welcome it at Makar Sankranti, with kites in Gujarat and sesame sweets shared with neighbors. A clock so large it holds the universe, and something beyond it that no clock touches.
screen: `A THOUSAND AGES FOR A DAY.` · `THE UNIVERSE BREATHES IN AND OUT.` · `BEYOND IT, WHAT NEVER PERISHES.` · `THE PATH OF LIGHT, THE PATH OF SMOKE.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Let your breath become a very small version of Brahma's day and night: on the in-breath, let sounds, thoughts and the feel of the room come forth; on the out-breath, let them dissolve back into quiet. In, the world appears; out, it rests. For the last few breaths, notice what doesn't come and go: the awareness watching both.
Uttarayana. The sun's northern course, what Bhishma waited for on his bed of arrows. A thousand ages each: the universe coming forth and dissolving, and beyond it, the eternal that never perishes.
Your line: the path of light and the path of smoke. The one who knows both isn't confused. Day one hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus consider uttarayana, the sun's northern course marked by the festival of Makar Sankranti, an auspicious time, and the Mahabharata's Bhishma is remembered for waiting for it before he died.

chat.meaning: Bhishma could choose his time, and waited for the sun to turn north. Gita 8.24 names that course on the path of light.
